newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO, Ukraine agree new security charter.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Ukraine agree new security charter.

text.p: NATO and Ukraine initialled a pact on Thursday marking a further stage in the redrawing of the security map of Europe.

The deal stops short of the landmark accord sealed with Russia on Tuesday when President Boris Yeltsin and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) agreed to the setting up of a permanent Russia-NATO Council.

But under the charter, which will be formally signed at a NATO summit in Madrid in July, the former Soviet republic of Ukraine will gain the right to call for "consultations" with the alliance if it feels under external threat.

"The charter gives expression to the special importance we attach to Ukraine as a democratic, independent state at the heart of Europe," said NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana at a special ceremony during a NATO foreign ministers meeting.

Ukraine, with international financial aid, is in the process of destroying its former Soviet nuclear weapons after declaring its intention to become a non-nuclear state. It has already removed the nuclear warheads from its SS19 and SS24 long-range missiles.

The NATO foreign ministers are laying the groundwork for the expected enlargement of the 16-country alliance to include some former members of the now disbanded Warsaw Pact, NATO's Cold War rival. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are front-runners to join.
With its NATO deal, Russia effectively agreed to the expansion, but it has said that it would not tolerate former Soviet repubics joining.
Ukraine is not seeking membership of the alliance but the pact initialled on Thursday marked the culmination of long negotiations on how to strengthen ties without arousing Russian ire.
"This is a very important document that is the result of three years of discussion," said Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko after initialling the accord.
The pact, officially called the "Charter on a Distinctive Partnership between NATO and the Ukraine", sets up a series of mechanisms for contacts between the two.
There will be an exchange of military missions, with NATO establishing an office in Kiev, while meetings at ambassadorial level will be held once a month.
A NATO-Ukraine Commission will get together twice a year and will provide the vehicle for the "consultations" at times of regional crises.
In the past two days there have been clear signs of a reduction in tension between the Ukraine and its former rulers in Moscow.
On Wednesday, the prime ministers of both countries said they had settled a dispute over a shareout of the former Soviet Black Sea fleet, defusing a potential threat to regional stability.
President Yeltsin is also due to make an oft-postponed first state visit to Ukraine on Friday and Saturday which is expected to result in the signing of a friendship treaty.
